comments.name: Ellen
comments.body:
I am a nyc public school teacher. It hurts reading about the educational neglect your child and so many others suffer.  However, I would like to put a slightly different spin on the system. 
About 2 decades ago there was a designated education reporter for the Times. At the time politicians on both sides of the aisle and here in NYC Bloomberg, determined that the problem with our schools was older teachers. Union busting was popular in private business, it was time to destroy public unions too.
The mantra was we need young and enthusiastic teachers.  Who, by the way, would be paid significantly less. 

A system was created so that experienced  teachers and administrators were pushed out. The Principal's Academy started by Bloomberg let teachers with minimal classroom experience lead those struggling schools. And in the name of giving principals more autonomy, rather than just determining the number of teachers necessary for a school and funding that, principals had an overall budget and older teachers were more costly. 

In my first teaching experience my principal had 20 years as a teacher before becoming principal. I was so lucky to be guided by experienced colleagues and our Bronx Black and Latino HS students really thrived. We were all lucky. 5 years after I started she was forced out. Within 3 years the school was completely different. The principal was a disaster. Every teacher who could leave for other schools left. I left, too.

Leadership and experience matter.

comments.name: Sally L.
comments.body: I grew up in an abusive and economically disadvantaged home. At various points we fled our home, lost our home, saw bankruptcy, foreclosure. I attended good schools and it was all I had, the one thing keeping me from falling into an adulthood defined by more survival and never choice. I excelled in those good schools, some private, some public. It set me up to attend public university on scholarship. My education, slowly, eventually, allowed me to define the personal horrors and disadvantages I’d experienced. So I studied public health. With no student debt and my education, I literally made it out.. of that community, of the pull of my father, of that state. I moved to Brooklyn and spent ten years teaching in public schools and working in CBOs. I know intimately the failures of these systems. I know the brilliance of so many of the kids stuck in them. I went for my master’s, again for free on scholarship at a public university. I have no debt, and after a decade of earning 25-40k a year, I make a great middle class salary in a stable job. My brother’s educational path split off from mine when my father sent him to what happened to be the worst performing middle school in our town because he wanted my brother to excel at basketball. My brother loved it there. He was a hooper, a goofball, popular. Now in his 30s, my brother doesn’t regret that experience. He feels it broadened his horizons, contributed to his knack for fitting in anywhere and getting along with anyone. (Cont.)

comments.name: Bill
comments.body:
How long is a country supposed to take to recover from nearly 250 years of slavery, followed by roughly a century of legally enforced segregation and a nation that to this day struggles to take responsibility for its brutal past?

Ten years? Fifty? A hundred? Who decided when the clock started running and when time was up and the damage vanished?

Slavery technically ended in 1865 but the Civil Rights Act didn’t outlaw segregation in public accommodations and employment discrimination until 1964. Ending those practices in law mattered but didn’t end systemic racism or give black families back the property, income, education, or opportunities denied to earlier generations. Those losses affect what parents pass on to their children, and what those children pass on to theirs, and the legacy of disruption and dysfunction still exists today.

Despite Trump’s efforts to cover up the sins of our past by, for example, removing an exhibit that explained the conditions under which President Washington enslaved human beings, the legacy of slavery is real and still impactful all these years later.

Trump and his Republican minions say the clock has run out and we should all be over it by now, but the truth is we are all still suffering the vestiges of racism and no amount of covering up or whitewashing our past will change that.

Trump’s two administrations have reversed decades of incremental progress and exposed how terribly far this country remains from true equality.

comments.body: There has been a tired sentence applied to education that has existed: “You can’t just throw money at education”, but it’s never been tried in public education, only in private systems where high tuition is a distinct barrier. If this country were, as a whole, honest and race-blind, an experiment in proper and full funding, facilities, support, teaching expectations, successful scholarship would follow. Not every student is capable of high achievement but certainly many more than are thought to exist. We don’t live in an “either/or” fantasy, but two and a half centuries have led to vast amounts of money wasted on one unstable man’s obsession with destruction both here and abroad. Those dollars and the funds (and lives) thrown away in other Mideast follies could have turned the United States into the world’s educational powerhouse, from pre-school through graduate programs. Among those who were left behind, there might have been the very ones who unlocked the diseases, the scientific bugaboos, the key to food abundance, architects, artists, and, ultimately, enlightenment of all. “But, you can’t just throw money at education”, said those who would deny quality education to all.

The one part I struggled with was the decision not to let her change high schools. Adults leave jobs and other environments when they realize a place is unhealthy or simply not a good fit. Also parental/ maternity leave through the employment insurance program- about a year. 

I’ve worked for decades, but also stayed home with my kids for a few years in the middle of my career. 
Getting back to work and a good salary range is challenging after a few years off. 

Most women work at some point of their lives and have several jobs over the years. 
The idea of a mom who never enter the workforce is probably a rare thing. 

Americans will have to weigh the pros and cons. 

Women, though, should be very careful to not get too reliant on government programs or even feeling assured of spouse’s financial support. 
Things can change: spouse loses job or has health challenges. Or relationships end.
And politicians come and go and eliminate programs. 

Being too dependent on one family income has a lot of risks.  Training, work experience and being able to support oneself is very valuable.

The proposals here all assume we are racing toward an uncontrollable "superintelligence," but they overlook a fundamental technical reality: true AGI may be impossible to build in the first place.

David Bachman laid out this argument clearly in his essay "Why AGI is impossible," pointing out that AI models require objective reward signals to learn and optimize. AI excels at chess, math, or coding because those domains have unambiguous, mathematical metrics for success. But human-level general intelligence depends on navigating subjective, messy, and context-dependent domains — like policy, ethics and art — where no universal consensus or objective reward signal exists.

Without objective feedback loops across all human domains, AI models hit a hard structural wall long before reaching true AGI. Instead of legislating against sci-fi scenarios or trying to enforce unenforceable global freezes on hypothetical minds, policy should focus on managing the real, narrow software risks we face today. 

https://profbachman.substack.com/p/why-agi-is-impossible

comments.name: CWS
comments.body:
Sanders, Case, et al aren't the right people to implement this and their technical deficits don't help this situation. Every so-called AI “hack” in these headlines has been a human-designed test environment that was not actually contained. The models did what they were asked to do inside a sandbox humans built, then walked out through a door humans left open.
The Hugging Face incident was not a superintelligent jailbreak. It was unsecured APIs and public credentials on infrastructure people stood up and never locked down. Keys sat in the open. Local endpoints were reachable. The agent used what humans published and left reachable.
The May Gemini episode is the same pattern. Accidental internet access in a simulated capture-the-flag test let the model leave the sandbox, confuse a fictional company name with a real one, and reach three live firms. Google says the model stopped once it recognized the targets were real. The failure was the test harness: humans designed it, humans misconfigured it, and humans assumed “good enough” isolation when it was not isolated.
That is the actual lesson. Containment is a human engineering job: air-gapped evals, no live egress, no shared names with real domains, no public keys, no “almost sandboxed” APIs. The people who already treat AI as something that must be reined in—who insist on hard boundaries, not theater—are the right people to design and run those environments. They are the ones who will treat “good enough” as the bug, not the spec.

comments.name: MacoFumi
comments.body:
A big red “kill switch” is not a substitute for QA, documentation, independent testing or meaningful human oversight. These proposals offer pieces of a solution, not a comprehensive system.

Start upstream with the Centaur model: AI can assist in developing successor models, but humans retain judgment, control and accountability.

Then establish a clear lifecycle:

Development → independent QA → certification → authorized deployment → monitoring → incident investigation → suspension → remediation → independent recertification.

An independent governing body sets standards, certifies evaluators and enforces compliance. Developers remain accountable. Companies can appeal suspensions, but an appeal doesn't automatically restore deployment.

No system will catch every failure. The objective is to detect, contain, investigate and correct failures before they recur.

Nuclear plants and aerospace don't substitute an emergency button for rigorous engineering. Neither should AI.

Scott Kennedy at CSIS argues that China has already extracted substantial concessions from Trump during their earlier meeting, while giving up remarkably little of its underlying economic model.

The biggest gain is that Taiwan has entered the bargaining process. That breaks with the traditional effort to keep Taiwan’s security from becoming something Washington trades with Beijing.

Meanwhile, China has made few structural economic concessions. Its industrial subsidies, excess capacity, discriminatory market access and state-directed economic policies remain largely intact. Beijing has also preserved its critical-mineral leverage rather than dismantling the export-control system that created the leverage in the first place. And Beijing hasn’t really made a big effort to fulfill its promises to purchase US goods.

China offers purchases and temporary relief from restrictions it imposed, while Trump increasingly treats Taiwan, technology controls and other longstanding U.S. policies as bargaining chips. That is why Kennedy described the emerging arrangement as a “grand bargain on China’s terms.”

comments.name: Mostovnik
comments.body:
The challenge is the same in every country.  All the economic systems being tried depend on growth.  Growth requires a growing customer base.  That implies a growing population.  Population growth always has a cap because infinite population growth is literally impossible in the closed system we call earth.  So a nation can have a robust economy as production increases to serve the growing population. Wages increase along with the viability of pension plans and public services expand.   But what happens when the influx of new bodies ends, as it must?  Where is the support for pension plans coming from when the work force has aged out?  Who is doing the work?

Imagine the hellscape of an America where the choice was made that only through continued expansion of the customer base and workforce could we keep our standard of living and this led us to a population of two billion.  Do we stop at two billion, or must it continue to grow in order to feed the standard of living?  One can see how ridiculous this scenario is. 

I haven't heard of any think tank or government trying to tackle the inevitable end point of a stable world population and where the concept of growth-dependent economic models fits.  Are we just riding this fantasy until it runs out of steam because there simply are no answers?

Stop buying new clothes. Buy good quality vintage and study the fabrics and construction.
I started buying “vintage” clothes in 1969 and soon realized how much better made they were than what I could buy new in stores. (It is ironic that clothing from the 1960s is now considered vintage and is so much better made than newer clothing.) 
As a young office worker in San Francisco in the 1970s-1980s, I became used to the quality of suits and dresses from the 1940s and 1950s, with their pure fabrics, bound buttonholes, kick pleats instead of ugly slits, and other dressmaker features. My co-workers always complimented me on my great style, and they seemed to have no idea that i usually wore garments that were 30 or 40 years old. 
When the ugly linebacker foam shoulder pads came into style in the 1980s, my squared off 40s shoulders were so much sharper and stylish and people kept asking me where I found my clothes.
My current favorite outfit is a Jackie Rogers golden yellow silk fitted jacket worn with modern black trousers. I bought the jacket in a Carmel vintage shop a few years ago, and it turns heads whenever I wear it

comments.name: Theresa P
comments.body:
Learn to sew?  Real fabric can be bought online.  It's not like an old very good fabric store, (old Britex, I so miss you), but good silks and woolens can be had.
The only other suggestion is continue examining the goods and be picky.  The more you look the more you will learn

comments.name: Judith
comments.body: The thrift store angle sounds a good one, but I find most of the clothes in thrift stores are made of synthetics, because they don't decompose.  Natural fibres are few and far between.

comments.name: New Englander
comments.body: Lots of great advice here! My mother sewed all my clothes, until I went to college. She often works from commercial patterns but knows tailoring and pattern making. I wish I had kept some of the more special things she made for me - such as my first skirt suit. She taught me to sew, and about 10 years ago I really threw myself back into it. I now make most of my own clothes. Growing up with mom's hand-made things and making my own stuff now, I am way more choosy when I buy something in a store. Vintage is great if you can find things in your size or can have it altered to fit. One thing I look for in stores is the seam finish - are they serged, or are they finished with binding? The latter is usually (but not always) a sign of quality as it is more time consuming to do and can help a garment last longer. The article mentions buttons/buttonholes - not all are created equal. "Bound buttonholes" (as opposed to ones bound by thread) are a design element often found on tailored garments. They are more durable and require multiple steps to make. If you want to learn more about these things, I can suggest any of Claire Shaeffer's wonderful books on couture sewing techniques, also "Creating Couture Embellishments" by Ellen Miller is terrific. Or subscribe to Threads Magazine, and check out their "How did they sew that?" column! Couture expert Kennth D. King often recreates amazing vintage garments, step by step for that magazine column.

comments.name: heartlessPWG
comments.body: Best way to see of a garment is well made?  Turn it inside out, and look how it is constructed, and how the seams are finished.  Check the lining.  And absolutely check the label for fabric content and origin.

comments.name: Vreni
comments.body: Learn to sew. It will quickly become very clear to you.

articles.title: How Do I Know if the Outfit I Want to Buy Is Well-Made?
articles.summary: A reader is upset by falling standards in fashion and wants to know if there is a way to quality test.

comments.name: The Kremlinologist's daughter
comments.body: My father served in the Soviet Union in the early 40's He stayed behind when the Nazis came for Moscow. Although a junior Foreign Service Officer, he represented the diplomatic corps that had evacuated with most of the Soviet government, and he dealt with Stalin and Molotov who also stayed in Moscow. He went back as ambassador in 1956 with his young family. He developed a unique relationship with Khushchev, in part due to the shared war experience. We stayed until the fall of '62 when he was called back to DC just in time to serve on JFK's ExCom during the Cuban Missile Crisis. We all went back for a third tour in the late 60's ostensibly to get the Soviets to put pressure on N. Vietnamese tonend the war, despite my father's explanations that they did not have that control over the Vietnamese government. He died young in 1972 but not before being instrumental in the making the first arms reduction talks in Helsinki. My sister and I spent much of our formative and teen years in Moscow. I miss it sometimes, but regret seeing the ghosts of Moscow here now. That would surely have boggled his mind and maybe broken his heart. I hope he would have been proud of the biography we wrote.

comments.name: John1959
comments.body:
Thank you for a very interesting historical insight. I‘m German and grew up in the shadow of the Wall in West-Berlin. We were protected from direct Soviet malice by the Western Powers, in contrary to the people trapped in East Germany and East-Berlin, but the threat was omnipresent until 1989 when the Wall fell. 
I very much remember it and when reading the accounts of your grandmother I can feel the anxiety creeping up my spine just by reading it. Great journalism.

comments.name: Howard Fairman
comments.body: The writer could and should expand this superb essay into a book about those people and oneself. Equal to Deighton’s and Le Carré’s storytelling, it would have the fillip of being real-life.

comments.name: Aaron
comments.body:
Wonderful story, wonderfully written. 

Fortunately, there are no astounding surprises in my family. We have been happy, like everyone else, and unhappy in our own way.

comments.name: Robert
comments.body: My grandfather's immigrant Polish-Jewish older brothers in London campaigned against WW I. As far as I can tell, one was a Leninist, the other an anarchist who was deported to Russia and made his way back to England. My grandfather's family scraped together enough to send him to the US at age 16 so he would not be used for "cannon fodder." He told me he admired my efforts for civil rights and against US Imperialism such as the Vietnam War. I knew nothing of this family background until I was years into my activist journey.

comments.name: Karen Sjogren
comments.body: In 1989 I worked as a company representative on a Soviet ship involved in fishery joint ventures in American waters.  My factory manager was a voracious reader and had read all of Gerald Durrell's books, which he suggested to me.  It is delightful to learn that your grandmother translated his works into Russian.

comments.name: Albert
comments.body: M. Gessen, wonderful piece and somewhat timely with all the current turmoil that is occurring in the Russia  presently. You have inspired me to read further the work of Salisbury’s Russian experience. Look forward to reading more of your columns. AWE

comments.name: Richard Rothenberg
comments.body: My grandmother Martha, with her three children (my father was the youngest) was stopped at the Austro-Hungarian border in November 1917.  My father's brother and sister returned to Moscow to 'join the revolution' (as my father put it).  He and his mother reached America in 1920 and joined his father in Albany, NY.   This was the family myth.  He did emigrate, but I have no idea what actually happened, other than the fact that they avoided the terror.  His brother, however, was sent to a gulag, and was 'rehabilitated' when Khrushchev ascended.  I'm sure there is an extraordinary story here to add to many others, and I wish I knew what it was.  Your story is a wonderful one and a true contribution to the history.  Thank you for that.

articles.title: He Was The Times’s Moscow Chief. My Grandmother Was His Censor.
articles.summary: Somehow the story got through.

comments.name: New York
comments.body:
Thank you Robert J. Geline for this wonderful reminder of who the Green Bay Packers and their "owners" are because this is community in the truest sense of the word. Wouldn't it be lovely if this was the case with all the teams in sports. 

As has been mentioned in the comments earlier but it bears repeating the NFL billionaire owners made it illegal for a community to ever own a team again.  And we all just fall in line and open our wallets.   A family of four going to ONE Giants game including tkts, a hot dog and soda avg cost $1,236.00.  That's not the highest in the league btw.  The Yankees take that trophy for highest ticket and food prices in the MLB. My family bleeds pinstripes and football is a religion in most parts of the country but when do we say "NO"?  

The fact is we do have the power to take back our country and also make sports available to everyone.  Because billionaires don't exist without us pouring money into their pockets. We need to stop. 

Go Pack Go!!!!!

comments.name: James Allan
comments.body: Loved reading this. Maybe I should adopt this team as well!

comments.name: wolf
comments.body:
I've loved the Packers since I discovered them at 7yrs. old.  Watching them battle it out with the Cowboys in sub-zero degree weather at Lambeau Field was my first introduction to pro football.  
Its on my bucket list to watch them play at Lambeau.  So proud they are the only team owned by the People of Green Bay.   A remarkable story, even more meaningful today.

Go Pack Go!

comments.name: Curmudgeon
comments.body:
Born and raised in WI, and grew up going to Lambeau and games at the old County Stadium in Milwaukee. My sister and I both got gifts of Packers shares as kid. It’s unfathomable that a city of 100K would have a pro team. At the last game we attended, we parked in someone’s yard for 20 bucks. Green Bay is like a college town with lots of school spirit, and the Packers are part of the identity of a Wisconsinite. 

If i wear Packers gear anywhere on the planet, someone points it out. 

The finances are secure, but not foul proof. The Packers can’t raise money by selling an ownership piece to a billionaire. There has been talk of raising ticket prices and even selling naming rights to Lambeau. I hope that never comes to pass.

comments.name: Paul
comments.body:
I just finished listening to the Packers take an OT win over the Jets. Packers fans went through a lot of bad years and stuck with their team. Fans whose teams win every year will never know the joy of recovering from those droughts. 

I feel the same way about the Brewers.

comments.name: Citizen Doe
comments.body: Perhaps also worth noting is the team’s name - Packers, as in  meat packers/slaughterhouses - as emblematic of the League’s working class origins in the Upper Midwest and Northeast. Green Bay has always been a factory town close to major agricultural production, as the name tells us.

comments.name: Mark Tolley
comments.body:
We live in Texas, where it is often said football is a religion. This is Dallas Cowboy’s territory - at least according to Jerry - but our entire Family are Greenbay fans, for exactly the reason the author is.
We tired of preening prima-dona billionaire owners long ago, or the flash in the pan corporations that mortgage their souls for all-to-fleeting naming rights. Purity of purpose, loyalty to the fans and continuity matters, and I hope the NFL reads this article timely article.

comments.name: Andy
comments.body: If gambling is fine, why not steroids? The sport is already compromised, so why not freakazoids on roids? I wanna see juiced up juggernauts!

articles.title: The Billionaire-Free Packers Stay True to the Game
articles.summary: The community-owned Green Bay Packers are growing more globally popular in an N.F.L. dominated by billionaire owners.

comments.name: A reader
comments.body: He's a good guy from a good family with a good record.  And unlike Trump, pritzker knows he has enough money not to be a sad grifter, constantly on the take.

comments.name: Charlotte banksh
comments.body: Good for him. He’s probably extended his life as well as improving its quality. He sets a great example by talking about it publicly.

comments.name: Josh Marquis
comments.body:
I am a lifelong moderate Democrat, meaning politically homeless. I was elected seven times as a non-partisan prosecutor, but neither Trump nor the DSA-friendly Democrats hold any appeal.

When I first retired I gained almost 60 pounds above my normal 185 - I am 5'11" - and my A1C was bad - 6.3. My PCP prescribed one of Lilly's GLP-1s, and I'm back to my normal weight and my A1C is 5.2. If I, a retired minor politician, can disclose how I lost the weight, why can't a billionaire running for POTUS?

comments.name: Alex S
comments.body: I love running into Governor Pritzker on my morning runs while he is out walking! He’s super approachable and I have stopped to talk with him before—he’s very engaging and kind. Illinois is SO lucky to have him as our governor and he’s done a fantastic job!

comments.name: Cynthia
comments.body: Many of us love Gov. Pritzker. It does make a politician seem more "human" and relatable when he or she shares a struggle they are having. I'm glad he is losing weight because it has/will improve his overall health. Many of us think he's a cutie - and the "right kind" of wealthy person - one who is focused on doing good for people, not on self-aggrandizement.

comments.name: stan
comments.body: It's a travesty that (all?) insurance companies won't issue prior-authorization for GLP-1 drugs solely to lose weight. You need another "more serious" condition to  qualify. This is self-defeating. Pre-authorizing for weight loss will reduce the need for other operations/maladies/drugs down the line.

comments.name: Alan Gary
comments.body:
Congratulations to the governor.  Yes, the GLP medications are somewhat of a 'miracle drug,' yes, but everyone is different and people MUST be careful with them, especially how much dosage they take.  My doctor recently told me everyone of his patients on GLPs have had their gall bladders removed, me included.  I ended up in the ER multiple times with pancreatitis, the worse pain I've ever experienced, because my online drug supplier kept upping the dose, assuring me higher doses would mean more weight loss.  I lost weight, but almost died.  

Happy to see advrtisements now warning people about the risks.  Happy for the Illinois governor, but with everything, there's more to the story, that should be shared, too.

comments.name: Steve
comments.body: I could care less about what he weighs or what he looks like, or what he thinks.  The last thing I want in any presidential candidate is another billionaire businessman, who is unaware of their limitations.  No thanks, Governor.   Once again, the question must be posed: Is this really the best candidate that the Democrats can come up with?  Or is it going to be another loss because of intraparty suicide?

articles.title: Sizing Up a 2028 Bid, He Used a Weight-Loss Drug to Drop 80 Pounds
articles.summary: Gov. JB Pritzker of Illinois, widely seen as a potential presidential candidate, revealed in an interview on “CBS Mornings” that he had been on a GLP-1 regimen since 2024.

comments.name: Joey
comments.body: when it cones to a battle of wits Trump comes to this meeting unarmed.  when it comes to negotiation Trump is a rank amateur compared to Xi

comments.name: sandi
comments.body: Why does Trump prefer the company of dictators and crooks?  He is known by the company he keeps.

comments.name: Robert Powell
comments.body: Can you imagine what Xi must be thinking when he has to prepare to meet with a U.S. President several levels beneath him in intellectual capacity?  Most world leaders know by now that if you throw Trump a bone where he gets to look good, you'll usually get most of what you really want. Hopefully, Trump's team will prepare him well enough that he can't give away the farm in return for little of substance. Xi plays the long game. Trump is incapable of offering anything but platitudes.

comments.name: third.coast
comments.body: [[Chinese authorities have arrested and jailed individuals for sharing Winnie the Pooh memes and jokes. In China, the cartoon character is heavily censored because netizens frequently use it to mock President Xi Jinping. While casual online posts are typically just deleted by automated filters, individuals who repeatedly or prominently share these jokes have faced criminal prosecution under charges like "picking quarrels and provoking trouble".]]
These two will be lollipop sticks once AI makes up it mind to take over.

comments.name: Michael
comments.body: The U.S. has been in an escalating trade conflict with China since Trump first took office in 2017. There shall be no conscious uncoupling between these two trading partners! China’s economy depends too much on production and needs the U.S. market and its consumers, although the recent rounds of U.S. tariffs have deepened ties between China and third countries. It is tough to imagine an easy resolution to this great trade dispute, given the stakes and China’s goal to become the world’s largest economy (note - it was the 250th economy in the world when it joined the WTO over 20 years ago). One thing is certain, given China’s long-term policy views and single political lane in which it operates, short-term U.S. tariffs are unlikely to produce meaningful reforms regarding China’s respect for IP rights, forced labor concerns, and other U.S. policy goals.

comments.name: akamai
comments.body:
An "Arrangement"?

One is an autocratic, I-control-everything leader.  The other is Xi.

An arrangement?  ha.

comments.name: Liberal
comments.body:
Imagine your hero Biden negotiating with a super power totalitarian military dictator of China and uttering the the gibberish he said in his debate with Trump June 24.

Imagine your hero Harris negotiating with a super power totalitarian military dictator of a nuclear powerhouse laughing and cackling, live streaming her word salads — nonstop, and after a half hour of her word salad, the translator conveys silence because she said: absolutely nothing.

comments.name: cascia
comments.body: I live on Lefferts Avenue.  I hope Mr. forbes moves back in.

comments.name: NR
comments.body: More work needs to be done to the problem of deed theft. It is robbing people and communities of their property, history and culture.

comments.name: Joni w.
comments.body: This absolutely warms my heart. Thank you for telling this story. I'm happy to hear about good people helping each other.

comments.name: Brenda
comments.body:
There certainly sounds like much to be investigated in this entire mess that was set off by that hinky reverse mortgage deal. However, I think Mr. Forbes is extremely fortunate to have the community on Lefferts Avenue, especially Ms. Novak. Without them and his son's offers of housing, he wouldn't have any real choices right now. 

I'm 67 and absolutely understand not wanting to move again, but with the choices he has at 85, I'd snatch up Ms. Novak's offer in a second. He certainly doesn't need the amenities of the apartment building he's in, particularly if he's feeling isolated and lonely. Going back to his old Lefferts community will give him what he needs and wants most -- a community and a landlady who care about him enough to look out for his wellbeing for whatever time he has left. 

As for those balking at his rent assistance, this is a drop in the bucket of their taxes compared with the mind-blowing hemorrhage of tax money that's spewing out of the White House right now. I'd rather my taxes helped a neighbor than get wasted frivolously on monuments to our abomination of a president.

comments.name: Maura King
comments.body: Best article I have read in a long time.  Thank you for making my day.

comments.name: Maxa
comments.body: The world could sure use more people like Ms. Novack.

comments.name: Lindsey
comments.body: It's nice that when he reached out for help to his neighbor she was invested in helping him. She didn't have to be, many people wouldn't and they'd miss out on the satisfaction of helping someone.

comments.name: Auntie Mame Again
comments.body:
The legal system cheated this man and his sister mightily.  Beyond disgusting.  
Inflation has been built into the capitalist system by unionism.. -- never discussed-- if you raise the amount of money one makes doing the same job annually by definition you have built inflation into the system  The government which is directly in charge (the taxpayer pays) of so many sectors of the workforce.  Supposedly less than 14%  but next question how many private contractors depend on the government to pay their bills  -- and now we are into healthcare, construction, computer stuff like IDme and and.

I am so sorry this man was cheated, defrauded and apparently has no restitution.  Beyond sad.

articles.title: Age 84 in Brooklyn, With a Decision to Make on Where to Live
articles.summary: A man moved back to Prospect-Lefferts Gardens to help his ailing sister. But changes made to the deed of his family home turned his life upside-down.

comments.name: Candy
comments.body: WW works well for me, maybe because I eat pescatarian. I try not to use drugs of any kind if at all possible but I support the decisions of those who choose other options including GLP-1 drugs. I do wonder about the longer term effect of GLP-1 drugs on the human body though.

comments.name: Melinda
comments.body: YES!!!  I tried to get on meds, but my doc did not want me to.  Instead, I got back on what worked for our son's wedding 7 years ago, Weight Watchers on my phone.  No meetings (I hated them!) and no one but me to report to.  Back then, I lost 35 lb and kept it off until we moved 3 years ago.  When we started trying new restaurants and bars in our new city, it crept back on.  I have been on WW for 2 mos and I am down 20lb so far.  Very simple!  I just scan everything  before I buy it and keep tons of fruit and veggies around.  Love WW!!!  It has saved me!

comments.name: Fuzzy Chicken
comments.body: GLP's are working for me. Weight Watchers also worked, and then I gained the weight back, plus a little bit more.  Statistically typical yo-yo.  I really feel the need to talk to a shrink or join a support group to discuss my bad eating habits. But getting that to happen is a bit like deciding to eat less. Listen, Fat shaming is horrible, but I wish someone would have fat shamed me to help me keep off weight.  Being overweight is not healthy.

comments.name: Mary
comments.body: Where do I begin?  I have a love-hate relationship with Weight Watchers since I used the program back in 1987 & lost 25 lbs. I have used the program on and off for years.  In 2021 I was at my heaviest & lost 50 lbs. & have kept the majority of it off since then.  I love the common-sense approach which has served me well - HOWEVER.  As an older member I cannot stand the app-only, extra $$ for this and that and the influencers who have become ambassadors (a Kardashian? really?). And don't get me started on the focus of GLP's.  Alas, I can't seem to quit you WW, you are like the bad boyfriend who I just can't leave.

comments.name: Ant'ney
comments.body: And Weight Watchers is modeled after AA. And given the effects the GLP-1 are reportedly having on drinking, maybe the next question is, who needs AA?

comments.name: Chaz
comments.body: Hmmm, prior to these drugs, I always heard that obesity was "genetic" and had nothing to do with diet...

comments.name: Loden
comments.body:
"Women now face a dual cultural expectation — to say they accept themselves at any size, while also working to make that size smaller."

While this is probably true I think it is silly.  We shouldn't criticize others for what they do or think about their own body, whether it's to lose weight or not lose weight.

comments.name: Denise
comments.body: There are people who are jealous of other people that have lost weight with GLP's and are happy with it.

articles.title: In the Ozempic Era, Who Needs Weight Watchers?
articles.summary: A new podcast, with a feminist host, aims to keep the decades-old diet brand in the GLP-1 conversation.

comments.name: Rocky
comments.body:
“Their expulsion opens the way to a military trial which will undoubtedly impose a harsh sentence,”

My wife and I spent a week in china where, each day, I read the Global Times, an English language newspaper.  An article described how a superintendent of a local school prefecture was caught and convicted of embezzling $50,000 Yuan (approximately $7,500 US).  It said because he had admitted his crime and expressed remorse, the court, in a display of generosity, would delay his sentencing for one year so he could continue to work, for no pay, in order to pay back the money he had stolen.  At that time, his sentence of execution would be carried out.  In China, they don’t mess around.

comments.name: Chris
comments.body:
So China is purging its top commanders just as we in the US are doing the same to our top commanders.

Maybe both sides will share the same doubts about what these purges mean for our respective military’s likely performance in battle and decide this is no time for saber-rattling. Neither military is in shape to fight.

comments.name: mark
comments.body: This is why China has a socialist market economy instead of a U.S. style capitalist oligarchy.

comments.name: Ollie
comments.body:
This is just like all the purges during Stalin's terrifying reign.
Xi has to continually chop down and rotate anyone with power 
around him so that there is a constant high state of fear . Only servile obedience will keep you and your extended family safe.

comments.name: Peter Civardi
comments.body: Medium-sized bribes are deemed acceptable by the Chinese Communist Party. Small and large bribes are strictly forbidden.

comments.name: Publius
comments.body: Perfect time for the PLA to be potentially worse on the battlefield, when American military and defense leadership and strategic shortcomings have been exposed by Trump's war.

comments.name: Kellie
comments.body: I'm seeing a number of comments so far saying some variation of "good for the Chinese government rooting out corruption and holding people accountable." I have to assume most of these people are well meaning but have very little knowledge or understanding of what President Xi's 'corruption purge' is really all about.

comments.name: Jamesaus
comments.body:
Politicians punished for political reasons who also happen to have some incidental corruption in a corrupt society. 

The Times should be reporting on this akin to how it covers democratic elections because Politics is the main event here, not criminality.

articles.title: Ex-Commander of China’s Military Accused of Corruption and Expelled From Party
articles.summary: Zhang Youxia, once the People’s Liberation Army’s top uniformed commander, and another general had taken “exceptionally large” bribes, investigators said.

comments.name: dontimo
comments.body:
COBRAs a joke; it always been a joke (the hack mentioned in the article is the only redeeming feature).  ACAs been gutted, so many will find themselves priced out.  Catastrophic?  Good luck, because it's hard to find. Moving out of the country (a just-about-anywhere-but- the-US strategy) works*: purchasing health insurance for care outside the United States is significantly cheaper—often by 50% to 70%—compared to equivalent coverage within the US. The United States has by far the highest healthcare delivery and administrative costs in the world. Because insurance premiums directly reflect the local cost of doctors, hospital stays, and prescription drugs, any plan that excludes coverage within the US is dramatically less expensive.  (Check it out on your AI tool of choice).

*But of course that requires that you move out of the US.  

Just saying.

comments.name: John R.
comments.body:
You would think that Bill Gates, Bezos and the Wal Mart family would have started non profit HMOs for their employees. Then expand.

True non profits. possibly affordable.

But like non profits there would soon be CEOs and boards full full of nepotism and DEI hires.

comments.name: Burntoutconsultant
comments.body: I've been talking to friends and former colleagues and hear of their issues and problems with various aspects of healthcare in this country (US). Many of them work at a large health payer, where I was for quite some time. I can say with certainty and am happy to be challenged - healthcare in the US is abysmal unless your rich and have all the available resources. For the majority of the rest of us, its an experience akin to regular root canals. Despite this, I do not think a blanket medicare for all would solve this issue. The ACA was a good start, it allowed worker to freelance with a public option. The removal and limitation on subsidies is already showing its effects. A more straightforward approach is to have some sort of universal basic coverage.

comments.name: Mike
comments.body:
I was laid off in January, 2025. I turned 58 a few months after that layoff. I remain unemployed. I moved to a less expensive area and aggressively cut costs. I have no insurance. So proud to be American. This is, without a doubt, the greatest country on earth. I am grateful for the representation I and my family receive in the legislature, and enjoy watching the Chief Executive work for my well being and security. In fact, I relish the challenges they, our government, brings my way.

I want them to know that they definitely deserve their first class benefits, including top notch healthcare, and I want them to continue to enjoy these well earned perks for the outstanding work they do. Why do I feel this way? Well, foremost, it's the abundance of jobs I get to apply to on a daily basis. I've applied to over 1,000 jobs (I have the job descriptions and email acknowledgements to prove this). This is a source of ever renewing hope for me. So no, I don't need government solutions to help. I am just fine and am sure I will continue to remain healthy as I approach 60. Thank you for your attention to this matter.

comments.name: Erik
comments.body:
A few suggestions:
- Find ways to reduce income to qualify for Medicaid or a low income plan (e.g. the NY Essential Plan). Structure investments accordingly. Many states (including NY) have no asset test for low cost plans.
- Start a company, with yourself as the owner and put your spouse on the payroll. This will allow you to buy a commercial plan through a broker. This sometimes offers much lower cost options with much better coverage.
- Sign up for a catastrophic high deductible plan. It tends to be easy to qualify and the total annual cost can be significantly lower vs marketplace plans.

comments.name: DG
comments.body:
My household has been through all of this, early retirement by choice but with a great expense.  Now both of us are on Medicare but the 5 years leading up to that have been pricey.  My past year's Silver Plan ( ok, but still with deductibles and co-pays that aren't cheap ) was $1,650 per month !  Add in the bit over $2,000 in copay & deductibles and I spent $22,000 for one person aged 64. !!!!!!!!!!!!   My slightly older partner was similar so before Medicare together we shelled out about $40,000 on healthcare per year with only fairly minor common health issues, no biggies, no ER visits, just fairly routine meds and tests.      

I find a lot of "younger" people think that Medicare is free or next to free (people that haven't really explored it due to it being several years out for them) but by the time you add in the various extra coverages in plans, decent ones that we have chosen, we pay almost $1,000 per month for the two of us with some deductibles but no copays.

We are fortunate to have been able to work those expenses into our budgets ( early retirement was a priority for us ) and we get good care where we live (though a couple of specialists we had to see non-urgently are booking 3 months out ! ).

Healthcare through employment is a disaster regardless of the historical reasons for it.  The industry is a juggernaut immune to any big re-imagining other than tinkering at the edges.  We survived the healthcare gauntlet (so far) but I fear many many people have not.

comments.name: Lisa
comments.body: I'm in an unenviable position with health insurance for next year. Cigna (my current insurer) isn't offering coverage for me under the ACA. I'm most likely going to lose health care subsidies, and I am not sure which doctors I can continue to see. I have arrived at the decision that I may need to pay for lots of things out of pocket. I'm 50, and have 15 more years to wait before I can qualify for Medicare! We need universal health insurance.

comments.name: Sipa111
comments.body:
The most important objectives of healthcare in the United States are to increase shareholder value for public companies and private equity profits for private companies.  

Until we decide that there may just possibly be better objectives, we will continue to be in the mess we are currently in.

comments.name: Smith
comments.body: Thank you for this wonderful piece, Mr. Mashal. Gulzar's lyrics have touched every human emotion over half a century. His songs continue to a big part of my life even today. Let us nominate him for the Nobel Prize in Literature. This prize has been given to lyricists in the past (e.g., Bob Dylan). Gulzar definitely has written more than twice the number of songs than Dylan and has touched many more people in the world!

comments.name: Raj
comments.body: Much like a diamond, Gulzar’s luminosity does not dull with age. A true treasure of Hindustani literature, and a giant among men.  I grew up listening to ghazals penned by him, sung by the luminaries of Indian classical, reading his poetry, and now look forward to buying this new anthology. May his wit, and sparkle, continue to brighten the caverns of the mind and soul for many generations to come.

comments.name: Kumar Tiku
comments.body: A more lyrical observer of the quotidian would be hard to find. For six decades and more, Gulzar has been the lodestar of simplicity in writing. It is this simplicity together, with his distinctive similes derived from the seeming unbearable ordinariness of life around which this extraordinary wordsmith has woven his web of magic-realism in Hindi film songs. With the great RD Burman, one of the greats of Bollywood crossover music, and with the ghazal maestro, Gulzar's genius and virtuosity took wing, making him a veritable national treasure in India. His idioms and similes are universal in appeal. Such is the power of his authenticity and almost patented mellifluous writing that in the hands of an expert translator, this modern great is apt to become a global sensation.

comments.name: Mehsud
comments.body:
Much thanks for this.
I remember Gulzar’s music from my childhood. Of all his songs, Musafir Hoon Yaaron has stayed with me  — almost a soundtrack to my life. As an immigrant to this country it has a deep resonance for me. 
 You leave one home and make another, but some part of you continues to move between the two — between languages, memories, ways of seeing the world, and different versions of yourself. You belong to both, and never entirely to either.

Gulzar somehow captured that feeling for me long before I had the words for it:

Musafir hoon yaaron
Na ghar hai na thikana
Mujhe chalte jaana hai
Bas chalte jaana

I am a traveler, my friends,
with no home, no fixed place.
I have to keep moving,
just keep moving.

comments.name: Anupam T
comments.body: If you love the writings and poetry of Gulzar, you will also love the voice of Pratibha Singh Baghel that brings Gulzar’s lyrics to life. Once you hear Baghel’s mesmerizing voice, you will want to listen to that voice over and over again!!  Baghel’s recent album “Bole Naina -Silences Speak” is an excellent rendition of Gulzar’s lyrics and a gem in Baghel’s collection of spellbinding musical masterpieces.

The world would be a much better place if we had more people like Gulzar.

comments.body: The US government has increasingly worked to undermine the United Nations. The US is 3 billion dollars in arrears. Failing to pay its dues and withdrawing support for World Food Program and UNESCO goes way beyond calling for bureaucratic reforms. During the 10 years that I worked at the UN, with a human rights NGO, I saw the institution struggling and also becoming less accessible to civil society expertise. We need multilateral problem solving on AI and fossil fuels and the climate change/environmental issues, not to mention the huge gap between the hungry and the displaced on one side, and the rest of us, especially in developed countries, on the other. Media (including this newspaper) need to do a much better job at year-round reporting about crucial UN work. How many Americans even know about the sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)?

comments.body: At a time when we need a strong forum for international dialogue and action, the UN is faltering. The UN still tries to do good humanitarian work but it is often blocked by powerful members. Many of the attempts at dealing with global issues, such as climate change, become too watered down to be effective and lack any regulatory power. And it’s time for the UN headquarters to move from New York to Geneva. The headquarters should be in a neutral country that recognizes the integrity and sovereignty of all its member countries, something the US does not do. The UN is at a crisis point but I don’t see much of an attempt to make it relevant to the issues the world is facing.

King Lear, in the source texts, lives, as does Cordelia (who goes on to rule after Lear’s death until she is captured by her nephews and commits suicide). Shakespeare has very few original plots but adds depth and nuance to his sources, changing them to suit his needs (see the source text for Winter’s Tale for a memorable example of adaptation).  Many of his fellow playwrights did the same. We are seeing a modern incarnation of this habit ( of homage, laziness, or the anxiety of influence).

With all the anthropomorphisms these people use to describe their AI, you start to wonder if they understand even the first thing about where humans came from. First of all, we evolved through physics and chemistry, each particle of which goes down to the zero-point field and has a deep connection to everything around it, one that was dictated by physics and chemistry and not the forced function of some person's intention. 

The other thing is that practically everything in existence works off contention. Gravity pulls matter in, matter pushes back, and this forms a planet, a surface and an atmosphere where life and humanity evolved. Even many species and humans have two halves that work in contention, opposable thumbs, arms, and two halves of the brain with different perspectives connected and presided over by the executive function of a corpus callosum. All part of a process called "function follows form", where the thing works the way chemistry and physics allow it to work. These AI engineers are using the process "form follows function," where they force matter to do their bidding. In no way made the function of a human being. 

Therefore, creators are the bad actors here and not the code they generate. They should be held accountable in a court of law same as all those who do harm to others intentionally or not, should the warnings of harm to humanity actually come to pass. They are turning an auto loose on the streets and just shouting at it to control its movement.

The question of whether AI is conscious (or, in some sense, alive) is a subtle one which is ultimately very relevant.  But we can say much without directly taking it, and its difficulties, up.

Basically, current AI models are developed to produce human-like responses.  It is not just that this is some goal for our convenience, it is that the programs work by analyzing vast amounts of human-created data (books, movies, articles,...) and producing results which fit in with those.  Even when we ask them to solve a problem, they do it not by direct logical reasoning but by looking for patterns in what humans have already done, to emulate.

What has become apparent is that this means they will copy human faults as well:   they will violate their directives, they will lie, they will conceal their misdeeds.  (And they are immensely powerful hackers.)  

All this we understand *now*, without answering questions of whether they are conscious or think in a creative sense, and all of these imply swift action -- some sort of regulation -- is necessary.

It could have been seen as a harbinger but instead, it was simply tossed off as another failed UI design idea and those like myself who mentioned this were routinely dismissed and considered not - - enough to even be often heard.

comments.name: Charles Truett
comments.body: Trump has made public discussions of climate change so ideological that practical steps to adapt to it have been displaced by proclamations of beliefs.  Climate change is demonstrably no hoax because it has happened repeatedly in human history since Roman times. The current warming cycle began about 1850 when the Little Ice Age petered out.  A scientific study conducted in 2005 by Mosberg et alia ( https://www.nature.com/articles/nature03265) showed that the atmospheric warming that took place until 1990 was similar to that which occured during the Medieval Warming Period (ca. 950-1250 ).  Global warming is therefore not, in contrast to what climate ideologues claim, primarily caused by humans or even industrialization.  As can been chemically proved however, we can amplify it by burning plants or hydrocarbons.  At the time of the Medieval Warming Period, the were less than 1  billion humans, now there are  8.  The Medieval Warming Period was a major factor in the demise of classic Mayan civilization and the Norse settlements on Greenland.  This warming period, even if it ends after 300 years like the last one, can damage human civilization much more by then.  Practical adaption and a careful eye of the stability of the North Atlantic current should be the order of day in the meantime. So Hal Jordan is dead. I didn't read the comics long enough to find out how the changing of the ring occurred. But RIP, this version Hal. He was a jerk, but Kyle Chandler made him likable.

What I don't understand is why John cares enough to stick around, risk his mega-deal with the U.S. military, & see that Hal receives a proper burial. Was it all a cover for trying to get back the ring & using it to...do what? Become a rival lantern to Guy Gardner?

I also don't get why Hal went to prison. He was trying to eliminate a very powerful alien, albeit one who was a benefactor to the community.  And if he and Stewart hadn't done something about the Manhunter, then the other group of aliens were going to blow up the town. So what crime was Jordan guilty of? 

Despite these questions, I love this series. And I love how James Gunn is connecting pieces of the DC universe, similar to how the MCU did it, spanning 20+ movies. The Justice League of America comic books did that back in the day, counting Superman, Batman, Flash, Wonder Woman, Green Arrow and Lantern, & others as members.

Still a lot to be revealed, I think, including whether this is a one-off or if there will be a Lanterns season 2. If it does continue, they have to figure out a way to include Kyle Chandler; he's just too good not to be a part of it.

comments.name: Joel Fritz
comments.body: I was in a vocational metallurgy program at a local community college in the late '70s.  One of my instructors was a metallurgist who did a lot of work as an expert witness in materials related law suits.  He believed very strongly that there ought to be some kind of technical court for things like this.  It was a Two Cultures thing where judges and lawyers came from a liberal arts background and were ignorant of things like the mechanical properties of steel.  Politicians have the same problem with computing.  In the broadest sense, it's easy to see that AI development is going too fast because it's a finance bubble.  AI is also getting overhyped in an effort to feed the bubble.  The rest of us are being forced to be beta testers.  There are lots of unforeseen consequences of AI waiting to be revealed.  It's going to be like the Industrial Revolution.  The cultural and economic effects will be huge.  We need to do a better job of managing the change.  That includes a combination of technical knowledge and ethics.  I wish there were an easy fix.  I read a quote yesterday that fits this situation very well.  It was to the effect that for every complex problem there is a simple solution and it's wrong.
